title: Diwali (5 days — Dhanteras, Naraka Chaturdashi, Lakshmi puja, Govardhan, Bhai Dooj)
hook: the darkest night, the brightest house: Lakshmi at the door, a mountain lifted, a sister's blessing
carry: Diwali (5 days — Dhanteras, Naraka Chaturdashi, Lakshmi puja, Govardhan, Bhai Dooj)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Diwali began: a clean house, something new on Dhanteras, a lamp for Yama, and Narakasura defeated before dawn. Did you clean one small corner? Day one hundred and forty.

Picture it from above. The night of the new moon, the darkest night of the month, no moon in the sky at all. And down below, a whole subcontinent, and neighborhoods from London to Singapore to New Jersey, lit up window by window, clay lamp by clay lamp, strings of lights on every balcony. The one night with no moon is the brightest night of the year. Somebody has left every door open. Somebody has drawn little footprints in colored powder, walking into the house. They're expecting a guest. Today, the last three days of Diwali.
screen: `THE NIGHT WITH NO MOON.` → `THE BRIGHTEST NIGHT OF THE YEAR.` → `FOOTPRINTS INTO THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Day three is Lakshmi puja, on the new moon itself, the main night for many families in North and West India. Lakshmi is the goddess of fortune and well-being, and the lamps are lit so she can find her way in. Those footprints drawn at the door are hers, walking toward the shrine. Ganesha is honored alongside her, first, as always: clear the road, then begin. Many business families bless their new account books that night, and in Gujarat the new year begins the next morning. In Bengal, the same night belongs to Kali, the fierce mother. Then the fireworks. Day four is Govardhan puja. The story: young Krishna persuaded the cowherds of Vraj to honor their own hill, Govardhan, which fed their cows, instead of the storm god Indra. Indra, offended, sent rain for days. And Krishna lifted the whole hill on one finger and held it up like an umbrella while everyone sheltered underneath. So temples build a mountain of food, called annakut, sometimes hundreds of dishes piled high, and share it. Day five is Bhai Dooj, for brothers and sisters. A sister marks her brother's forehead with a tilak, prays for his long life, and feeds him; he gives her a gift. The story behind it is that Yama, lord of death, visited his sister Yamuna on this day and was welcomed with a meal. Notice the bookends. Diwali opened with a lamp for Yama, asking death to pass by. It closes with Yama as a brother, sitting down to eat. Five days: a clean house, darkness beaten, fortune welcomed, shelter under a lifted mountain, and family at the table.
screen: `LAKSHMI PUJA: THE DOORS LEFT OPEN.` · `GOVARDHAN: THE HILL LIFTED ON ONE FINGER.` · `BHAI DOOJ: A SISTER'S BLESSING.` · `YAMA AT THE START AND AT THE END.`

segments.voice: If you can, light a small lamp or candle and set it near your door, or picture one there, glowing outward. Sit facing it. Now think of someone who is like a brother or sister to you: a sibling, a cousin, a friend who's been family. Picture them clearly. Wish them a long life, and well-being, the way a sister does on Bhai Dooj. If you pray, you can hold their name before whatever form you honor. Then just sit with the light at the door. The bell holds the time.
Diwali. Five days of light: something new, darkness defeated, Lakshmi welcomed on the darkest night, a mountain lifted, and siblings at the table. Today's word.

Your line: Diwali, five days: Dhanteras, Naraka Chaturdashi, Lakshmi puja, Govardhan, Bhai Dooj. Today, send one message to someone who's like a sibling to you, wishing them a long life. Day one hundred and forty.

howItsDone: On the new-moon night of Diwali many Hindu families perform Lakshmi puja with Ganesha, light lamps throughout the home and draw Lakshmi's footprints at the door; the next day temples offer annakut for Govardhan puja, and on Bhai Dooj sisters mark their brothers' foreheads with tilak and share a meal.

fork.setup: you're a cowherd in Vraj. the storm god is furious, and it's been pouring for days. the young Krishna says, come under here. what happens?
options: he leads everyone into a cave.
he lifts the whole hill on one finger to shelter them.
he asks Indra to stop the rain.
fork.reveal: he holds up Govardhan like an umbrella while everyone and their cows shelter underneath. temples remember it with annakut, a mountain of food.

original.note: Sanskrit lakṣmī: fortune, prosperity, well-being; the goddess welcomed on Diwali night.

trapdoor: what you thought: fireworks and sweets.
what it means: five days that move from a clean house to darkness defeated, fortune welcomed, shelter given and family fed.

what a scholar hears: Govardhan's lifting is told in Bhagavata Purana 10.24–25; the Yama–Yamuna story behind Bhai Dooj (Yama Dvitiya) is found in later Puranic and regional tradition; Bengal keeps Kali puja on the same new moon.

sources.ref: Lakshmi puja and Yama Dvitiya (Bhai Dooj), as kept in household and regional tradition
